items.purpose: The earned value status report tells the sponsor and the change-control board where Project Beacon stands on cost and schedule at a fixed status date, why, and what they must decide. The Programme Manager writes it from the reconciled programme register (khn_programme_register.csv) and the schedule. Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer and change-control board chair, checks the figures, and Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), the executive sponsor, receives and accepts it at the monthly steering meeting, or sooner when a threshold is breached. This one reports status at 2026-10-01. It practises the PMP Process tasks Evaluate project status and Plan and manage finance.

sections.heading: Status summary
sections.guidance: Open with four or five sentences a busy sponsor can act on: the overall rating, earned value (EV) against planned value (PV) and actual cost (AC), the forecast at completion against the budget and the reserve, the gate at risk and the decision you need. State the rule behind the rating so the colour is not an opinion. It is good when the sponsor could stop reading here and still make the right call.

sections.heading: Data basis and reconciliation
sections.guidance: Name the source file, the status date and every cleaning rule that changed a number: the duplicate WP-104 removed, the WP-113 sign error corrected, WP-101 capped at 100%. Show that the budget at completion (BAC) adds to CAD 1,200,000 and name the wrong totals people get (CAD 1,220,000 and CAD 1,080,000). It is good when another analyst can reproduce every figure from the file.

sections.heading: Earned value measures
sections.guidance: Put PV, EV, AC, cost variance (CV), schedule variance (SV), the cost performance index (CPI) and the schedule performance index (SPI) in one table with the formula, the value and a plain-words meaning. CV and SV are always EV minus something, and an index below 1.00 is unfavourable. Add percent complete (EV / BAC) and percent spent (AC / BAC) so readers see the gap.

sections.heading: Forecasts
sections.guidance: Show the estimate at completion (EAC), estimate to complete (ETC), variance at completion (VAC) and the to-complete performance index (TCPI). Say which EAC formula you report and why, and give the other formulas as a range. Compare the EAC with the BAC and with the total authorized funding including the management reserve. It is good when the reader sees how much better the team must perform on the remaining work.

sections.heading: Variance by work package
sections.guidance: Break the totals down by work package so causes are visible. List each work package that has PV, EV or AC, with its CV and SV, and add a total row that matches the headline figures. Name the one or two work packages that explain most of the variance instead of spreading the blame evenly.

sections.heading: Schedule and critical path
sections.guidance: SPI measures value, not time. Check the critical path in the schedule (khn_schedule.csv) before you decide what is urgent: a large SV on a task with float can matter less than a small one on the critical path. Name the gate at risk and the task that threatens it, using the dates and float from the schedule.

sections.heading: Risks, issues and corrective actions
sections.guidance: Link the numbers to the RAID log: which risk the variance raises (R-08) and which issues it exposes, such as a work package with no owner. List corrective actions with an owner and a date, and label them proposed until the change-control board or sponsor decides. Never add cost or move a baseline inside a status report; that goes through change control.

sections.heading: Decisions requested
sections.guidance: End with a numbered list of decisions, each with who decides and by when, plus the next status date. A status report that asks for nothing while the forecast exceeds the reserve has not done its job.

| Document ID | BCN-R2-17 |
| Title | Earned value status report |
| Owner | Programme Manager |
| Approver | Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), executive sponsor |
| Reviewed by | Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer and change-control board chair |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Date | 2026-10-02 (status date 2026-10-01) |
| Status | Issued to the steering meeting |

## Status summary

Overall: Red (Beacon reporting rule, proposed: Red when the cost performance index (CPI) or schedule performance index (SPI) is below 0.90). By 2026-10-01 Beacon planned CAD 278,900 of work, earned CAD 224,000 and spent CAD 250,600. At today's cost efficiency the programme finishes at CAD 1,342,500: CAD 142,500 over budget and CAD 22,500 more than the total authorized funding of CAD 1,320,000, so the management reserve would not cover it. The Release 1 go-live gate (2026-10-23) is at risk. Decisions needed: approve the recovery actions and name an owner for WP-108.

## Data basis and reconciliation

Source: khn_programme_register.csv, reconciled to the approved figures. 16 rows; the duplicate WP-104 row is removed, leaving 15 work packages. WP-113's budget of -60,000 is corrected to 60,000 (Finance confirmed a sign error). WP-101's 110% complete is capped at 100% (status Complete). Budget at completion (BAC): CAD 1,200,000 (Release 1 420,000; Release 2 460,000; Release 3 320,000). Rejected totals: 1,220,000 (every row) and 1,080,000 (duplicate removed, sign not fixed). The CAD 120,000 management reserve is held by the sponsor outside the register.

## Earned value measures

| Measure | Formula | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Planned value (PV) | budget x planned % | CAD 278,900 | Work scheduled by 2026-10-01 |
| Earned value (EV) | budget x % complete | CAD 224,000 | Work done, at budget rates |
| Actual cost (AC) | ledger | CAD 250,600 | What that work cost |
| Cost variance (CV) | EV - AC | CAD -26,600 | Over cost |
| Schedule variance (SV) | EV - PV | CAD -54,900 | Behind plan |
| CPI | EV / AC | 0.89 | 89 cents of work per dollar |
| SPI | EV / PV | 0.80 | 80% of planned work done |

Progress: 18.7% complete (EV / BAC) against 20.9% of the budget spent (AC / BAC).

## Forecasts

| Forecast | Formula | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Estimate at completion (EAC) | BAC / CPI | CAD 1,342,500 |
| Estimate to complete (ETC) | EAC - AC | CAD 1,091,900 |
| Variance at completion (VAC) | BAC - EAC | CAD -142,500 |
| To-complete performance index (TCPI) to finish on BAC | (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) | 1.03 |
| TCPI to finish on total authorized funding | (BAC - EV) / (1,320,000 - AC) | 0.91 |
| TCPI to finish on the EAC | (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC) | 0.89 (equals today's CPI) |

We report BAC / CPI because every work package with costs to date has a CPI below 1.00 (0.78 to 0.97): the overrun is spread, not a one-off. Range for the steering meeting: if it were a one-off, EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = CAD 1,226,600; if cost and schedule pressure both continue, EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) = CAD 1,610,113. Finishing on budget needs a CPI of 1.03 on the remaining work; even spending the whole reserve needs 0.91, better than today.

## Variance by work package

| Work package | PV | EV | AC | CV | SV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WP-101 Mobilization and charter | 40,000 | 40,000 | 41,200 | -1,200 | 0 |
| WP-102 Privacy impact assessment and threat model | 70,000 | 63,000 | 68,500 | -5,500 | -7,000 |
| WP-103 Profiling, data quality, warehouse staging | 101,400 | 78,000 | 92,300 | -14,300 | -23,400 |
| WP-104 Semantic model, dashboards, row-level security | 0 | 7,000 | 9,000 | -2,000 | 7,000 |
| WP-106 Role catalogue and role-based access control design | 67,500 | 36,000 | 39,600 | -3,600 | -31,500 |
| Total | 278,900 | 224,000 | 250,600 | -26,600 | -54,900 |

WP-103 causes 54% of the cost variance. WP-103 and WP-106 cause all of the schedule variance; WP-102's -7,000 and WP-104's early start of +7,000 cancel out.

## Schedule and critical path

WP-102 is 90% complete against 100% planned, and it holds schedule task 4 (Complete privacy impact assessment): critical path, zero float, due 2026-09-24. Task 6 (warehouse staging, in WP-103) is also critical, cannot start until tasks 4 and 5 finish, and is due 2026-10-06. Tasks 8, 9 and 11 follow with no float, so any slip reaches the Release 1 gate. WP-106 has the largest SV, but its task 13 has 14 working days of total float (late finish 2026-10-23), so it threatens no gate yet.

Calendar note: the schedule has no statutory holidays. Remembrance Day (2026-11-11) is the first day of critical task 17; adding it moves the Release 2 gate to 2026-11-27. Thanksgiving (2026-10-12) falls in critical task 8; adding both moves the Release 1 gate to 2026-10-26 and the Release 2 gate to 2026-11-30.

## Risks, issues and corrective actions

- R-08 (owner Marcus Bell, E-002): the forecast now exceeds the reserve by CAD 22,500. Recommend raising its rating to High.
- New issue: WP-108 (multi-factor authentication and single sign-on rollout, CAD 130,000, starts 2026-10-26) has no owner in the register.

| Action (proposed) | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Close the remaining WP-102 work, task 4 first because it is critical | Priya Raman (E-003) | 2026-10-05 |
| Options to recover task 6 (add a second analyst), with cost for the board | Tomás Rivera (E-006) | 2026-10-07 |
| Confirm WP-106 finishes inside its float | Daniel Osei (E-004) | 2026-10-09 |
| Bottom-up re-estimate of Releases 2 and 3 | Programme Manager | 2026-10-16 |

## Decisions requested

1. Sponsor (E-001): name an accountable owner for WP-108 before 2026-10-26.
2. Change-control board (E-002): approve the actions above and decide the task 6 recovery option on 2026-10-07.
3. Sponsor: note the forecast is CAD 22,500 above total authorized funding. No reserve release is requested today; the re-estimate on 2026-10-16 will say whether scope, schedule or funding must change. Next status date: 2026-10-30.
mistakes: Getting a sign backwards. CV is EV minus AC and SV is EV minus PV, so a negative number or an index below 1.00 is bad news. Writing CV as AC minus EV turns an overrun into an apparent saving.
Totalling the register without cleaning it. That gives a BAC of CAD 1,220,000 or CAD 1,080,000 instead of CAD 1,200,000, and every forecast built on it is wrong.

Treating SPI as the schedule verdict. WP-106 has the largest schedule variance but 14 days of float, while late WP-102 holds the privacy impact assessment task on the critical path and threatens the Release 1 gate.

Comparing the EAC only with the BAC, or treating the management reserve as the Programme Manager's money. Only the sponsor can release the reserve, so a forecast above total authorized funding goes to the sponsor as a decision.

items.purpose: The service desk knowledge and escalation model gives the service desk reusable knowledge articles, clear escalation paths and measurable targets for clinician access issues, so a clinician gets working access fast and security or privacy events reach the right person at once. Grace Liu (E-005), IT Service Desk Manager and owner of the access service, writes it with the Programme Manager; Daniel Osei (E-004) and Priya Raman (E-003) check the security and privacy routes; Marcus Bell (E-002) approves it. Analysts use it on every access call from the start of the multi-factor authentication (MFA) and single sign-on (SSO) rollout. It practises ITIL knowledge management and the Support stage, and the PMP tasks Plan and manage project compliance, Support organizational change and Help ensure knowledge transfer.

sections.heading: Scope and baseline demand
sections.guidance: Say which contacts the model covers and measure today's demand from khn_service_desk.csv: access requests by system, their median days and target performance, and the contacts the desk already handles well (password resets). It is good when the numbers show where knowledge will save the most waiting.

sections.heading: Support tiers and roles
sections.guidance: Lay out tier 0 (self-help) to tier 3 (specialists and vendors) with named people or groups and what each tier does. State the segregation-of-duties rule for access: the business owner approves, the provisioner never does. A good table lets a new analyst see where any ticket goes next.

sections.heading: Knowledge article catalogue
sections.guidance: List each article with an ID, a title in the caller's words, the tier that resolves it and a named owner. Tie each one to a real pattern in the data, such as the mover with leftover access (E-028) or the agency nurse past contract end (E-014). An article nobody owns will go stale.

sections.heading: Article standard
sections.guidance: Give one template every article follows (symptom, applies to, cause, steps, confirmation, escalation, security and privacy notes, owner, review date, linked known error) and show one complete article as an example. Judge it by whether a new analyst could follow it on a night shift without asking anyone.

sections.heading: Escalation paths
sections.guidance: Separate functional escalation (moving work to the right skills) from hierarchical escalation (moving a decision to someone with authority), and give security and privacy events their own immediate routes. Name people, triggers and channels. Label any internal timing as Kestrel policy, not law.

sections.heading: Targets and measures
sections.guidance: Show each measure with its baseline from the data and its target, labelling charter targets as agreed and new ones as proposed. Include the existing resolution targets by priority (P1 4 hours, P2 8 hours, P3 24 hours, P4 72 hours) and at least one knowledge measure, such as tickets closed with a linked article.

sections.heading: Compliance and review
sections.guidance: Record the rules that keep the desk compliant: least information under the Health Information Act (HIA), identity checks before resets, no credentials by email. Set a review cycle and the training needed before go-live, so knowledge transfer is planned rather than hoped for.

| Owner | Grace Liu (E-005), IT Service Desk Manager |
| Approver | Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer |

| Status | Final, in use from 2026-10-26 (start of the sign-in rollout) |

## Scope and baseline demand

Covers every contact about clinician access to the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001), the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) and the Beacon dashboards (A-009), including multi-factor authentication (MFA) and single sign-on (SSO). Baseline from khn_service_desk.csv (219 unique tickets):

| Contact | Tickets | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Access requests: CIS access | 36 | Median 4.16 days |
| Access requests: Virtual desktop | 7 | Median 4.19 days |
| Access requests: Power BI | 6 | Median 4.40 days |
| All access requests | 49 (44 resolved) | Median 4.26 days; 27.3% within 72 hours; target met 15.2% |
| Password resets (service requests) | 27 | All within target; median 0.72 hours |
| Virtual desktop incidents | 31 | Includes all 4 P1 incidents |

Password resets show the desk resolves fast when the steps are written down. Access requests stall: none of the 16 P3 access requests with a known outcome met its 24-hour target, and access requests as a whole (all priorities) score 3.05 of 5 for satisfaction (19 responses) against 3.50 for all tickets.

## Support tiers and roles

| Tier | Who | Does |
|---|---|---|
| 0 Self-help | Portal on the IT Service Management Platform (A-011) | Request status, MFA enrolment guide, published articles |
| 1 Service desk | Noah Bergstrom (E-031), Zainab Yusuf (E-032); lead Grace Liu (E-005) | Log, verify identity, apply articles, resets, route |
| 2 Resolver groups | Identity and Access; Clinical Applications; End User Computing; Analytics Support | Provision roles; fix CIS, virtual desktop and dashboard faults |
| 3 Specialists and vendors | Ahmed Haddad (E-017), Lucas Girard (E-033); Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01); NorthArc Cloud (V-02) | Platform faults and vendor defects |

The system's business owner approves access; the person who provisions never approves (segregation of duties, issue I-01).

## Knowledge article catalogue

| ID | Article | Resolves at | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| KB-ACC-01 | New clinician needs CIS access (joiner) | Tier 1 logs; Identity and Access provisions | Identity and Access lead |
| KB-ACC-02 | Role change (mover): add the new role, remove the old | Identity and Access | Identity and Access lead |
| KB-ACC-03 | Agency nurse access (ClearPath Staffing, V-03) | Tier 1, with end date | Grace Liu (E-005) |
| KB-ACC-04 | Vendor remote support access (V-01) | Tier 2, approved by Daniel Osei (E-004) | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| KB-ACC-05 | MFA enrolment, new or lost phone | Tier 1 | Grace Liu (E-005) |
| KB-ACC-06 | SSO or virtual desktop sign-in fails on a shared workstation | Tier 1, then End User Computing | End User Computing lead |
| KB-ACC-07 | "I can't see my site" on the Beacon dashboards | Analytics Support | Tomás Rivera (E-006) |
| KB-ACC-08 | Account still active for someone who has left | Tier 1 to security, same hour | Sam Okafor (E-020) |
| KB-ACC-09 | Password reset | Tier 1 | Grace Liu (E-005) |

Each one answers a real pattern: KB-ACC-02 from E-028's leftover Unit Clerk access, KB-ACC-03 from E-014, KB-ACC-04 from E-015 (privileged, no MFA, no end date), KB-ACC-08 from E-014 and E-027.

## Article standard

Every article has: a title in the caller's words; symptom; applies to (systems, roles, sites); cause; steps; how to confirm it worked; when and where to escalate; security and privacy notes; owner; review date; linked problem or known error.

Example, KB-ACC-03 Agency nurse access:
1. Confirm the unit manager made the request and ClearPath Staffing sent the placement with start and end dates.
2. Verify identity against the HR record (A-015), never against patient details.
3. Log the end date; the account expires on it automatically.
4. Route to Identity and Access for the Agency Nurse role.
5. Confirm sign-in and MFA on the first shift.
Security note: no end date, no account.

## Escalation paths

- Functional (to skills): Tier 1 escalates when no article fits, the article fails, or the fix needs rights the desk does not hold.
- Hierarchical (to authority, Kestrel rule, proposed): analysts alert Grace Liu at once for P1 and P2, and when any ticket reaches 75% of its target with no plan; Grace Liu alerts Marcus Bell when a P1 misses its target.
- Security: a suspected compromise, an active leaver account or unexpected privileged access goes to Sam Okafor (E-020) by phone immediately. He engages Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) and classifies it.
- Privacy: if anyone may have seen health information they should not, the analyst tells the Privacy Office (Priya Raman, E-003) the same shift. Under the Health Information Act (HIA) an affiliate, which includes every employee, must tell the custodian; this route is how the desk does that.

## Targets and measures

| Measure | Baseline | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Access requests resolved within 72 hours | 27.3% | 80% (agreed, charter) |
| Median days to fulfil an access request | 4.26 | 1 (agreed, charter) |
| Resolution targets | P1 4 h, P2 8 h, P3 24 h, P4 72 h | Unchanged |
| Password resets within target | 27 of 27 | Hold at 100% (proposed) |
| Tickets closed with a linked article | Not recorded | Baseline in November, then set (proposed) |

## Compliance and review

- The HIA requires the least amount of health information needed (section 58): articles never ask for patient details or put them in tickets.
- Check identity against HR data before any reset or MFA change; never send passwords or codes by email.
- Every article is reviewed every six months and after any process or system change (proposed).
- Grace Liu trains every analyst on KB-ACC-01 to KB-ACC-08 before 2026-10-26.
mistakes: Writing articles from memory instead of from ticket patterns, so the desk gets articles nobody needs and none for Clinical Information System (CIS) access requests, which are most of the demand.
Treating escalation as one path. Functional escalation moves work to skills, hierarchical escalation moves a decision to authority, and security and privacy events need their own fast routes.
Letting the desk widen access to settle a complaint, such as changing row-level security for someone who cannot see a site. The article must route it to the data owner instead.
Publishing articles with no owner or review date, so they go out of date as soon as MFA and single sign-on change the sign-in steps.

items.purpose: The Release 2 closure report confirms that Release 2 (clinician identity and access) was accepted, records what was delivered and changed, reports schedule and cost, sets out the access benefits as baselines with agreed targets to be measured three months later, hands the access service to named operational owners, and captures lessons. The Programme Manager writes it the day after the Release 2 acceptance gate (2026-11-26); Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) approves it, Daniel Osei (E-004) confirms the security items, and Grace Liu (E-005) confirms the service handover. It feeds the programme closure report. It practises the PMP tasks Manage project closure and Help ensure knowledge transfer, and the ITIL move from Transition into Operate, Deliver and Support.

sections.heading: Acceptance decision
sections.guidance: State who accepted the release, on what date and against which criteria and evidence (the user-acceptance test scripts and the security acceptance criteria). Name any conditions. A signature without criteria is not acceptance; it is a hope.

sections.heading: Scope delivered and changes
sections.guidance: List the work packages with owners and budgets, confirm the deliverables are filed, and record every approved change with its decision and impact (here CR-01). Check the budgets add to the Release 2 figure of CAD 460,000. A reader should see exactly what was and was not delivered.

sections.heading: Schedule and cost
sections.guidance: Compare the gate date with the baseline and name the critical path tasks. For cost, give the budget at completion and the latest reconciled figures, and say plainly how and when the final actual cost will be confirmed. Never fill a gap with an estimate presented as a result.

sections.heading: Benefits: baselines and targets
sections.guidance: Benefits come after the release, so report each access measure with its baseline from the data, its agreed target, who measures it, the evidence source and the measurement date three months after acceptance. Say in one sentence that no benefit is claimed yet. Inventing early results is the fastest way to lose the sponsor's trust.

sections.heading: Service handover
sections.guidance: Give every part of the new service a named operational owner and say what was handed over: catalogue entry, knowledge articles, workflows, dashboard. Add any early life support period. "Handed to IT" is not a handover; a person who accepts the work is.

sections.heading: Open risks, issues and actions
sections.guidance: List every risk and issue still open, its status at closure and who owns it afterwards, including items carried into Release 3. Closing a release does not close its risks; it moves them to an owner who will watch them.

sections.heading: Lessons learned
sections.guidance: Record a few specific lessons with the evidence behind them and an action with an owner, written about conditions and decisions rather than people. Use real Release 2 events: the team conflict, CR-01 and the identity data problems.

sections.heading: Risks, dependencies and assumptions

sections.heading: Governance and approval

## Objectives and success criteria

Objective: keep caring for patients through a cyber attack and recover clinical systems within business-approved targets. Charter measure: Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001) restore within its 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO). Baseline (data): failed, 9.0 h and 13.5 h, last test 2025-08-14. Target (agreed): pass, measured three months after the release.

Acceptance criteria: business impact analysis signed by each tier 1 owner; RTO and recovery point objective (RPO) approved for every tier 1 system; a CIS restore passes within 4 hours; tabletop run and playbook updated; overdue vulnerabilities fixed or under approved exceptions; security-operations dashboard live; SEC-004 major-incident review done.

Approach: predictive, because gate dates are fixed and tasks depend on each other, with feedback loops: the tabletop updates the playbook; a failed restore feeds a fix and retest.

Business impact analysis method:
1. Scope tier 1 and tier 2 services from the inventory (A-005 needs an owner first).

items.purpose: The network segmentation and logging design divides Kestrel's network into zones, lists the only flows allowed between them (everything else denied), and specifies the log sources, routing and retention that the managed security operations centre (SOC), Sentinel SOC Services (V-04), and Kestrel need to detect and investigate attacks. Its aim is to stop ransomware spreading and to cut detection time. Ahmed Haddad (E-017) designs the segmentation, Sam Okafor (E-020) the logging; Priya Raman (E-003) reviews the privacy of logs leaving Canada; Daniel Osei (E-004) approves it before any firewall change goes to the change-control board. It practises the CISSP domains Communication and Network Security (secure design principles in network architectures) and Security Operations (logging and monitoring).

sections.heading: Design goals and principles
sections.guidance: Say what the design must achieve in Kestrel terms (contain ransomware, protect backups, detect faster) and the principles behind it: deny by default, least privilege, defence in depth. Anchor the goals in data, such as the 25.29-hour mean time to detect.

sections.heading: Zones
sections.guidance: Group systems from the inventory into zones by trust and function, with clinical core, management, user access, workstations, analytics and external zones. Put an unsupported system such as A-014 in its own quarantine zone. Every system ID should appear in exactly one zone.

sections.heading: Allowed flows
sections.guidance: List each permitted flow with an ID, source zone, destination, what is allowed and the control on it, then state that all other traffic is denied and logged. A good flow table lets a firewall engineer build rules and an auditor test them without asking questions.

sections.heading: Administrative and vendor access
sections.guidance: Describe how administrators and vendors reach systems: jump hosts, multi-factor authentication (MFA), approved and time-limited sessions, recording, and separate backup administration. Note current gaps from the data, such as privileged accounts without MFA, and make fixing them a condition of go-live.

sections.heading: Log sources
sections.guidance: For each source say which events to collect and why, tied to real incidents where you can. Cover identity, clinical audit logs, virtual desktop, endpoints, firewalls, backups, email, the Power BI activity log and vendor sessions.

sections.heading: Log routing, privacy and retention
sections.guidance: Say where logs go, how time is synchronized and how long they are kept, labelling retention periods as Kestrel policy. When logs leave Canada, apply the Health Information Act: safeguards under section 60, minimize what is sent, and decide whether the privacy impact assessment must be updated and submitted before the feed starts.

sections.heading: Detection use cases and measures
sections.guidance: Turn the logs into a few named detections, each with its signal and response, and set a detection target labelled as proposed. Without use cases, logging only creates storage costs.

sections.heading: Implementation and testing
sections.guidance: Give the rollout order, the change-control route and the tests that prove the design works, including negative tests that must fail. Starting new rules in monitor-only mode avoids blocking a clinical flow nobody documented.

| Title | Network segmentation and logging design |
| Owner | Ahmed Haddad (E-017), Network Engineer; logging: Sam Okafor (E-020) |
| Approver | Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Date | 2026-10-02 (data as of 2026-10-01) |
| Status | Final; privacy reviewed by E-003 |

## Design goals and principles

- Stop ransomware spreading from user devices to clinical servers and backups. Critical precursor SEC-004 hit the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008).
- Deny by default: a flow not in the table is blocked and logged.
- Least privilege between zones; administration only from the management zone with multi-factor authentication (MFA).
- Defence in depth: segmentation, MFA, endpoint protection and logging each catch what the others miss.
- Detect faster: mean time to detect (MTTD) was 25.29 hours (9 valid incidents); SEC-003 took 84.08.

## Zones

| Zone | Contains | Trust |
|---|---|---|
| Z1 Clinical core | A-001, A-002, A-003, A-005, A-006 | Restricted; highest protection |
| Z2 Imaging | A-004 and imaging devices | Restricted |
| Z3 Legacy quarantine | A-014 (past end of support) | Isolated |
| Z4 Management and identity | A-007, admin jump hosts, log collector | Administrators only |
| Z5 User access | A-008 virtual desktop hosts | Clinician sessions |
| Z6 Workstations | Shared clinical workstations, staff devices | Untrusted by default |
| Z7 Analytics | A-010 warehouse, on-premises data gateway | Restricted staging, Confidential views |
| External | NorthArc Cloud (A-011, A-012, A-013, A-015), Power BI service (A-009), Sentinel SOC Services (V-04), vendors | Defined flows only |

## Allowed flows

| ID | From | To | Allowed | Control |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FL-01 | Z6 | Z5 | Virtual desktop sessions | MFA and single sign-on through A-007 |
| FL-02 | Z5 | Z1, Z2 | Clinical application clients | Desktop pool only; no workstation reaches Z1 |
| FL-03 | Z1 | Z1 | Interfaces between clinical systems | Named servers only |
| FL-04 | Z1, Z2, Z5, Z7 | Z4 | Authentication to A-007 | Directory traffic only |
| FL-05 | Z1 | Z7 | Scheduled extracts to staging | Read-only service account |
| FL-06 | Z7 gateway | Power BI service | Outbound encrypted web traffic (port 443) | Gateway opens every connection |
| FL-07 | Z1, Z2, Z4, Z7 | A-012 | Backup traffic, one way | Console only from Z4; immutable copy (CT-005) |
| FL-08 | Z4 collector | V-04 | Filtered security events, encrypted | See privacy controls |
| FL-09 | V-01, V-02 | Z4 jump host | Remote support | MFA, approved ticket, time limit, recorded |
| FL-10 | Z3 | Paging gateway | A-014 messaging only | Nothing else in or out |

## Administrative and vendor access

- Administrators work only from Z4 jump hosts with MFA. Privileged MFA is 66.7% today (E-009 and E-015 not enrolled): fix before go-live.
- Vendor sessions need a ticket approved by the system owner, end the same shift (proposed) and are recorded.
- Backup administration uses accounts outside the main directory, so a stolen directory credential cannot delete backups.

## Log sources

| Source | Events | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A-007 Identity Directory | Sign-ins, failures, MFA and privileged group changes, account create and disable | SEC-009; missed leavers |
| A-001 Clinical Information System (CIS) audit log | User, role, date, time, action, record accessed | SEC-003; privacy investigations |
| A-008 Virtual Desktop | Session start and end, source device | SEC-002, SEC-004, SEC-008 |
| Endpoint protection | Malware, mass file changes, encryption behaviour | Ransomware precursors |
| Zone firewalls | Allowed and denied flows | Lateral movement |
| A-012 Backup Platform | Job results, deletions, retention changes | Attackers target backups |
| A-013 Email | Reported phishing, clicked links | SEC-001, SEC-007, SEC-010 |
| A-009 Power BI activity log | Sharing, export, workspace role changes | SEC-006 |
| Vendor sessions | Start, end, user, ticket | Supplier access |

## Log routing, privacy and retention

- All sources feed the Z4 collector on one synchronized time source; SEC-008's impossible sequence shows what bad timestamps do to an investigation.
- Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) processes logs in the United States (risk R-05, owner Priya Raman, E-003). No Alberta statute bans this, but the Health Information Act (HIA) section 60 requires safeguards for health information stored or used outside Alberta. Design: forward security events only; replace patient identifiers in CIS audit events with a pseudonymous token; keep full CIS audit logs in Canada; contract terms limit use (Kestrel contract requirement).
- Priya Raman decides whether the privacy impact assessment needs updating; if so, it goes to the Information and Privacy Commissioner for review and comment before the feed starts (HIA section 64).
- Retention (Kestrel policy, proposed): security logs 1 year; CIS access logs 10 years, the period the provincial logging standard sets for Alberta electronic health record access logs.

## Detection use cases and measures

- Ransomware precursor: mass file changes, backup deletion attempt or new admin account; Critical, isolate the zone.
- Privileged misuse: admin sign-in outside Z4 or self-granted rights; High.
- Record snooping: a CIS user opening many records outside their unit; Privacy Office review.
- Leaver account used: sign-in by an account HR marks terminated; High, disable.
Target (proposed): Critical and High incidents detected within 1 hour, against the 25.29-hour MTTD baseline.

## Implementation and testing

- Firewall changes go through the change-control board in agreed change windows (the week 9 gateway lesson).
- Order (proposed): Z4 first, then Z3 for A-014, then Z1 and Z5 rules in monitor-only mode for a week before blocking.
- Tests: a Z6 workstation must fail to reach Z1; the backup console must refuse a Z1 connection; every log source must appear at the collector.
mistakes: Allowing workstations to reach clinical servers directly "for now". One infected workstation can then reach the CIS, which is how ransomware spreads.
Putting backup administration in the main directory, so the same stolen credential that encrypts the servers can also delete the backups.
Sending full clinical audit logs to a SOC in the United States without minimization, contract safeguards or a privacy decision under the Health Information Act.
Collecting every log without detection use cases or time synchronization, so the SOC has data but cannot build a reliable timeline.

items.purpose: The incident classification model gives the service desk, Sentinel SOC Services (V-04), security and privacy one shared way to decide whether something is a security incident, its category, severity and priority, its response targets and who is told, so the same event gets the same response at 03:00 as at noon. Daniel Osei (E-004) owns it, built with Sam Okafor (E-020), Grace Liu (E-005) to align with service desk priorities and Priya Raman (E-003) for privacy triggers; Marcus Bell (E-002) approves it. It is tested against the ten real incidents and in the tabletop exercise. It practises incident management in the CISSP Security Operations domain and ITIL prioritization by impact and urgency.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.guidance: Define event, alert, security incident, possible privacy breach and major incident in one line each, so people stop arguing about words during a crisis. Make clear that a possible privacy breach always reaches the Privacy Office whatever its severity.

sections.heading: Categories

sections.heading: Severity criteria
sections.guidance: Write criteria for Critical, High, Medium and Low against patient care and service impact and against information impact, with a real Kestrel example in each row. Add the tie-break rule (highest column wins; when unsure, go one level up). Criteria must be observable, not "feels serious".

sections.heading: Priority and response targets
sections.guidance: Combine severity with urgency to get a priority, reuse the service desk codes P1 to P4 and their existing resolution targets, and add security response times labelled as proposed. Give the current baseline, such as the 1.93-hour mean time to contain, so targets are realistic.

sections.guidance: Name who is told at once and who is told next, and how soon, for each severity, using real names and IDs that match the escalation matrix, and point to the escalation and breach-notification matrix for channels, timings and legal duties. Keep this table short so it can be read in seconds.

sections.heading: Privacy and breach triggers
sections.guidance: Explain that privacy is assessed separately from severity: health information goes to a risk-of-harm assessment under the Health Information Act, staff personal information to a real-risk-of-significant-harm assessment under the Protection of Privacy Act. Show how a Low service incident can still be a notifiable breach.

sections.heading: Worked examples and calibration
sections.guidance: Apply the model to the real incidents and compare with the severity recorded. Where the record disagrees with the model, or similar incidents got different severities with no reason, say so. This table is the proof that the model works.

| Title | Incident classification model |
| Owner | Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer |
| Approver | Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Date | 2026-10-02 (data as of 2026-10-01) |

## Definitions

- Event: anything observable, such as a sign-in or a blocked email.
- Alert: an event a tool or person flags as possibly harmful.
- Security incident: an event that harms or threatens the confidentiality, integrity or availability of Kestrel systems or information, or breaks Kestrel security policy.
- Possible privacy breach: any loss of, or unauthorized access to or disclosure of, health or personal information. It always goes to the Privacy Office, whatever its severity.
- Major incident: any Critical incident, or any incident that stops a tier 1 clinical service at a site.

## Categories

Keep the categories already used in khn_security_events.csv so trends stay comparable: Phishing, Malware, Ransomware precursor, Unauthorized access, Misconfiguration, Lost device. Add Ransomware (encryption confirmed) and Data exfiltration. One primary category per incident; if analysis shows a different cause, change it and log the reason.

## Severity criteria

| Severity | Patient care and service | Information | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | Tier 1 clinical service down or at imminent risk at a site or more | Restricted data encrypted, copied or destroyed at scale | SEC-004 ransomware precursor on A-008 |
| High | Tier 1 system affected but care continues; privileged account compromised | Confirmed unauthorized access to Restricted or Confidential data | SEC-003 on the Clinical Information System (CIS); SEC-009 on the directory |
| Medium | Tier 2 or 3 system, or one tier 1 device, contained | No confirmed access to Restricted data | SEC-002 malware on one virtual desktop |
| Low | One user, no service impact | Nothing exposed | SEC-010 phishing reported and blocked |

Rule: the highest row any column reaches sets the severity. When unsure, classify one level higher and lower it later with evidence.

## Priority and response targets

Priority combines severity with urgency (spreading, or a shift or clinic about to start) and uses the service desk codes so one queue works.

| Priority | Usually | Triage | Containment started | Service restored |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Critical, or High and spreading | 15 minutes | 1 hour | 4 hours |
| P2 | High | 30 minutes | 4 hours | 8 hours |
| P3 | Medium | 4 hours | 24 hours | 24 hours |
| P4 | Low | Next business day | 72 hours | 72 hours |

Triage and containment times are proposed. The restore column uses the existing desk targets (P1 4 h, P2 8 h, P3 24 h, P4 72 h); for a security incident it means service back with a workaround, while full recovery is tracked separately. Baseline: mean time to contain 1.93 hours over 9 valid incidents.

## Escalation by severity

| Severity | Told at once | Told next |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Sam Okafor (E-020), Daniel Osei (E-004), Marcus Bell (E-002), Grace Liu (E-005) as major-incident manager, Chloe Dubois (E-016) for downtime, Priya Raman (E-003) | Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), within 1 hour |
| High | E-020, E-004, the system custodian | E-002 the same day |
| Medium | E-020 and the resolver group | E-004 in the daily summary |
| Low | E-020 queue | Weekly report |

Contact methods, timings and legal steps are in the escalation and breach-notification matrix.

## Privacy and breach triggers

Privacy is assessed separately from severity. Any incident touching Restricted data (individually identifying health information) goes to Priya Raman (E-003) for a risk-of-harm assessment under the Health Information Act (HIA). Any incident touching staff personal information, such as the Identity Directory or the HR and Payroll System, goes for a real-risk-of-significant-harm assessment under the Protection of Privacy Act (POPA). A Low incident can still be a notifiable breach: a lost unencrypted phone holding a patient list is Low for service and serious for privacy.

## Worked examples and calibration

| Incident | Recorded | Model result | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-004 Ransomware precursor, A-008 | Critical | Critical, P1, major incident | Matches |
| SEC-003 Unauthorized access, A-001 | High | High, P2, HIA trigger | Matches; 84.08 h to detect |
| SEC-009 Unauthorized access, A-007 | High | High; Critical if a privileged account was used; POPA trigger | Contained, not recovered at 2026-10-01 |
| SEC-001, SEC-007, SEC-010 Phishing, A-013 | High, Medium, Low | High if credentials were entered; Low if reported and blocked | Three severities, no recorded reason |
| SEC-005 Lost device, A-013 | Low | Low only if encrypted and no health information on it | Check the record |
| SEC-008 Malware, A-008 | Medium | Medium | Fix the impossible times |

## Reclassification and review

Anyone may raise a severity. Only Sam Okafor (E-020) or Daniel Osei (E-004) may lower one, and the reason is logged. Every incident records the criterion that set its severity. The model is reviewed after the tabletop exercise (task 23) and every six months (proposed).
mistakes: Setting severity by gut feel. The three phishing incidents on email were recorded High, Medium and Low with no reason, which a written criterion would have prevented.
Folding privacy into severity, so a Low incident such as a lost device never reaches the Privacy Office even when it held health information.
Inventing a separate priority scale for security, so the service desk and the SOC work from two queues with different meanings of P1.
Letting anyone downgrade an incident without a logged reason, which hides risk from the people who must decide.

items.purpose: The ransomware response playbook gives Kestrel step-by-step actions, named roles and decision rights for a ransomware attack, from preparation through detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons, with clinical downtime built in. It follows the NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 incident handling phases and notes that Rev. 3 (April 2025) superseded it. Daniel Osei (E-004) owns it as incident commander; Sam Okafor (E-020) and Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) run the technical work; Chloe Dubois (E-016) owns clinical continuity; Marcus Bell (E-002) approves it. It is used whenever a Critical ransomware incident is declared and is tested in the week 12 tabletop. It practises the CISSP Security Operations domain (incident management, recovery) and ITIL incident management.

sections.heading: Scope, framework and activation
sections.guidance: Say what the playbook covers, which framework structures it and why, and exactly what activates it and who may do so. Name NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 and its four phases, and note that Rev. 3 (April 2025) superseded it and maps to the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions. A playbook nobody knows how to start is not used.

sections.heading: Roles and decision rights
sections.guidance: Name a person for each role, including vendors, and say which decisions each may take. The hardest decisions (taking the Clinical Information System offline, contact with the attacker) must sit with named executives, not be left for the night shift.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.guidance: List the prerequisites with their real state from the data and an owner: immutable backups, restore test results, MFA on privileged accounts, overdue vulnerabilities, downtime procedures, printed contact lists. Showing failed prerequisites honestly tells leaders where the plan is weakest.

sections.heading: Detection and analysis
sections.guidance: Write a numbered first-hour checklist: confirm, classify, scope, preserve evidence, escalate. Include a benchmark from a real incident (SEC-004) so the team knows the speed to aim for. Steps must be short enough to follow under stress.

sections.heading: Containment
sections.guidance: Give the short-term containment actions in order, protect the backups, and spell out the clinical decision to take a tier 1 system offline and who triggers downtime procedures. Require a log of every action, because the timeline matters for recovery and for privacy notification.

sections.heading: Eradication
sections.guidance: Say how to find and close the entry point, rebuild rather than clean, reset credentials in the right order and confirm the weakness is patched. Skipping eradication is why organizations get hit twice.

sections.heading: Recovery
sections.guidance: Restore in a dependency order taken from the system inventory, check the recovery point and integrity, get business-owner confirmation before ending downtime, and watch for reinfection. Be honest when a recovery target has not been proven by a test.

sections.heading: Post-incident activity
sections.guidance: Set when the blameless review and the major-incident review happen, which times to measure and compare, which documents to update and how the playbook is tested. Lessons only count when they change a document or a control.

## Scope, framework and activation

Covers suspected or confirmed ransomware on any Kestrel system, from the first precursor to the lessons review. The steps follow the four phases of NIST Special Publication 800-61 Rev. 2: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity. NIST superseded Rev. 2 with Rev. 3 in April 2025, which arranges incident response around the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover). Kestrel keeps the Rev. 2 phases because they map straight to actions: preparation sits mainly under Govern, Identify and Protect, then Detect, Respond and Recover.

Activation: any Critical incident in the Ransomware precursor or Ransomware category, or an encryption alert on a tier 1 system. Sam Okafor (E-020) or Daniel Osei (E-004) activates it at any hour.

## Roles and decision rights

| Role | Person | Decides or does |
|---|---|---|
| Incident commander | Daniel Osei (E-004) | Runs the response; moves between phases |
| Technical lead | Sam Okafor (E-020) with Sentinel SOC Services (V-04) | Analysis, containment actions, evidence |
| Infrastructure | Ahmed Haddad (E-017), Lucas Girard (E-033) | Isolation, rebuild, restore |
| Clinical continuity | Chloe Dubois (E-016) with Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) | Downtime procedures, clinical priorities |
| Privacy | Priya Raman (E-003) | Breach assessment and notification |
| Communications | Grace Liu (E-005) | Major-incident updates to staff |
| Executive | Marcus Bell (E-002), Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) | Taking tier 1 systems offline; any contact with the attacker |
| Vendors | Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01), NorthArc Cloud (V-02) | Clinical Information System (CIS) fixes; backup restores |

Kestrel position (proposed for executive approval): plan to recover without paying. Any decision to engage with the attacker is made by the executive with legal advice and police involvement.

## Preparation

| Prerequisite | State at 2026-10-01 | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Immutable CIS backup copy in Canada | Pass (CT-005) | Kevin Park (E-009) |
| CIS restore within its 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO) | Failed: 9.0 h (CT-001), 13.5 h (CT-002); last test 2025-08-14 | Chloe Dubois (E-016) |
| Multi-factor authentication (MFA) on privileged accounts | 4 of 6; E-009 and E-015 not enrolled | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| Overdue vulnerabilities | SEC-012 (CIS), SEC-015 (paging), SEC-017 (imaging) | Sam Okafor (E-020) |
| Paper downtime procedures in every unit | Not yet written; due in WP-112 (task 22) | Chloe Dubois (E-016) |
| Printed playbook and phone tree at each site | Proposed | Grace Liu (E-005) |

The phone tree is printed because email (A-013), the Identity Directory (A-007) and paging (A-014) may all fail together: paging depends on the directory.

## Detection and analysis

First 60 minutes:
1. Confirm the signs: encryption alerts, ransom notes, mass file renames, backup deletion attempts, new administrator accounts.
2. Classify Critical, P1, major incident. Open one record and start a timeline on one clock.
3. Scope: which zones, systems and accounts; which tier 1 services are hit (use the system inventory).
4. Preserve evidence: isolate affected machines rather than wiping or powering them off; keep memory and logs.
5. Call the escalation matrix contacts. The Privacy Office joins at once because health information may be affected.
Benchmark: SEC-004 (2026-08-11) was detected 0.75 hours after it began and contained 2.67 hours after detection.

## Containment

- Isolate affected zones at the firewall; disconnect the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) pool if it is the source; disable compromised accounts; block known indicators.
- Protect the Backup Platform (A-012): suspend deletion rights and confirm the immutable copy.
- If the CIS (A-001) is hit or at risk, the incident commander recommends and the executive decides whether to take it offline. Chloe Dubois starts downtime procedures in emergency, lab, pharmacy and inpatient units.
- Log every action with time and person.

## Eradication

- Find the entry point (phishing, an unpatched weakness, vendor access) and close it.
- Rebuild affected servers from known-good images; never just clean an encrypted host.
- Reset privileged and service account credentials first, then all users in affected zones, with MFA enforced.
- Patch the weakness that was used and rescan.

## Recovery

- Restore in the inventory order: A-007; A-012 and A-014; A-008 and A-001; then A-002, A-003, A-005; then tier 2 and tier 3.
- Use the last clean backup; check the recovery point (CIS: 1 hour) and data integrity before users return.
- The business owner confirms data and function before downtime ends; paper records are entered afterwards.
- Watch for reinfection for two weeks with extra logging (proposed).
- Until a CIS restore passes (risk R-04), plan for a CIS outage longer than 4 hours.

## Post-incident activity

- Blameless post-incident review within 10 working days (proposed), plus the major-incident service restoration review led by Grace Liu (E-005).
- Record time to detect, contain and recover; compare with SEC-004, recovered 2026-08-13 18:30, 63.42 hours after detection.
- Update this playbook, the classification model and the risk register; track every action to an owner.
- Tabletop test: encryption of the CIS on a weekday at 07:00 (task 23, 2026-12-04 to 2026-12-10).
mistakes: Wiping or powering off infected machines straight away, which destroys the evidence needed to find the entry point and to judge whether health information was taken.
Assuming backups will save the day. The Clinical Information System (CIS) has failed both restore tests, so the playbook must plan for an outage longer than its 4-hour target until a restore passes.
Keeping the playbook and contact list only on systems the attack may encrypt, such as email or the file share.
Leaving the decisions to take the CIS offline or to deal with the attacker unassigned, so they are argued about while the attack spreads.

items.purpose: The incident and problem management workflow defines how Kestrel restores service quickly through incident management, including major incidents, while problem management finds and removes underlying causes, and how both connect to security response, change control and knowledge. Grace Liu (E-005), IT Service Desk Manager, owns it and runs the weekly problem review; resolver group leads own individual problems; Sam Okafor (E-020) owns the security interface; Marcus Bell (E-002) approves it. Every analyst and resolver uses it daily. It practises the ITIL incident management and problem management practices across the Operate and Support stages, and incident management in the CISSP Security Operations domain.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.guidance: State the different goals of incident management (restore fast) and problem management (remove causes), what the workflow covers, and where it sits in the product and service lifecycle. Add a baseline from the service desk data so improvement can be measured later.

sections.heading: Incident workflow
sections.guidance: Give the steps from logging to closure as a numbered list, with the priority targets and the point where a known error or article is checked. Show both kinds of escalation. Closure must capture the cause code and linked problem, or trend analysis has nothing to work with.

sections.heading: Major incidents
sections.guidance: Define what makes an incident major, who manages it, how often clinical leaders hear from you, and how it hands over to the ransomware playbook when security is involved. Separating the person who communicates from the person who fixes keeps both jobs done.

sections.heading: Security incident interface
sections.guidance: Say how the desk hands a suspected security event to the security team, what it must not do to the device, and how the two records stay linked with consistent times. Use the data quality problems in the security records to show why checks before closure matter.

sections.heading: Problem management workflow
sections.guidance: Describe problem identification, problem control and error control in plain steps, including workarounds, known errors and the change route for the permanent fix. Every problem needs a named owner and a review rhythm.

sections.heading: Current problem records
sections.guidance: Open real problem records from the data, each with evidence (ticket counts, security events, control tests) and an owner, and mark which are known errors. This proves the workflow works on Kestrel's actual pain points rather than examples.

## Purpose and scope

Incident management restores normal service as fast as possible. Problem management finds and removes the causes so incidents stop coming back. This workflow covers every incident in the IT Service Management Platform (A-011), including security incidents passed on by Sentinel SOC Services (V-04). In the product and service lifecycle it sits in Support and Operate; permanent fixes go through Transition by change control.

Baseline (khn_service_desk.csv, 2026-08-01 to 2026-09-30): 113 incidents; median resolution 14.4 hours; 76.4% met target; incidents by priority P1 100.0%, P2 76.0%, P3 72.7%, P4 80.8%; 5.9% of all tickets reopened.

## Incident workflow

1. Log: every call, email or alert gets a ticket with site, system (asset ID) and category.
2. Prioritize: impact and urgency give P1 to P4, with resolution targets of 4, 8, 24 and 72 hours. Security categories use the incident classification model.
3. Match: search known errors and knowledge articles; apply a workaround if one exists.
4. Diagnose and escalate: functional escalation to the resolver group; hierarchical escalation to Grace Liu at 75% of target (proposed).
5. Resolve: restore service and confirm with the user.
6. Close: final category, cause code and any linked problem.

## Major incidents

Declared when a tier 1 clinical service is down at a site, a P1 affects many users, or a Critical security incident occurs. Grace Liu (E-005) is major-incident manager and owns communication; a separate technical lead fixes. Clinical leaders get updates every 30 minutes (proposed) through the desk, or the printed phone tree if email is down. A security major incident runs under the ransomware playbook with Daniel Osei (E-004) as incident commander. Every major incident ends with a major-incident review.

## Security incident interface

- The desk passes any suspected security event to Sam Okafor (E-020) at once, and does not wipe, reimage or power off a device until the security operations centre agrees, because evidence matters.
- One A-011 ticket links to the security case, holding occurred, detected, contained and recovered times.
- Records are checked before closing: SEC-008 shows containment before detection, and SEC-005 was entered twice.

## Problem management workflow

ITIL describes problem management in three phases:
1. Problem identification: weekly trend review of incidents, repeat incidents, major incidents, supplier notices and vulnerability findings.
2. Problem control: analyze causes (timeline, five whys), document a workaround, and record a known error when the cause is known but not yet fixed.
3. Error control: remove the known error through a change (the change-control board for Beacon systems), then confirm the incidents stop.
Every problem has a named technical owner. Grace Liu chairs a weekly problem review (proposed).

## Current problem records

| ID | Problem | Evidence | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| PRB-01 | Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) instability and malware | 31 incidents including all 4 P1s; SEC-002, SEC-004, SEC-008 | Ahmed Haddad (E-017) |
| PRB-02 | Repeat phishing on Email and Collaboration (A-013) | SEC-001, SEC-007, SEC-010; agency and vendor awareness training 48% | Sam Okafor (E-020) |
| PRB-03 | Clinical Information System (CIS) restore exceeds its 4-hour recovery time objective | CT-001 9.0 h, database rebuild ran long; CT-002 13.5 h, runbook out of date | Chloe Dubois (E-016) |
| PRB-04 | CIS faults | 30 incidents: 6 missed target, 3 reopened | Clinical Applications lead with Meridian (V-01) |

PRB-03 is a known error: the causes are recorded but not fixed. Its workaround is the paper downtime procedure, and the fix and retest sit in Release 3 task 22.

## Measures and review

| Measure | Baseline | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Incidents resolved within target | 76.4% | 90% (proposed) |
| Tickets reopened | 5.9% | Under 3% (proposed) |
| Problems with a named owner | New | 100% |
| Known errors with a workaround in the knowledge base | New | 100% |
| Repeat incidents after a problem is closed | New | Measured monthly |

Grace Liu reviews these monthly with Marcus Bell (E-002) and records improvements in the continual-improvement register.
mistakes: Keeping an incident open until the root cause is fixed. The incident closes when service is restored; the cause is pursued in a linked problem record.
Closing incidents with no cause code or category check, so repeat failures such as the 31 virtual desktop incidents never show up as a trend.
Letting the desk reimage an infected machine before security has collected evidence.
Recording a workaround and calling the problem solved. A known error stays open until a change removes the cause and incidents stop.

items.purpose: The escalation and breach-notification matrix says who is told about an incident, by whom, how fast and through which channel, from first detection to the statutory notices required by Alberta privacy law. It separates Kestrel's internal rules from legal duties under the Health Information Act (HIA) and the Protection of Privacy Act (POPA). Daniel Osei (E-004) owns the escalation rows and Priya Raman (E-003), Chief Privacy Officer, owns the privacy rows; Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) approves it. Everyone on an incident uses it, and it is tested in the tabletop. It practises the CISSP Security and Risk Management domain (legal and regulatory compliance) and Security Operations (incident management), and the PMP task Plan and manage communication.

sections.heading: How to use the matrix
sections.guidance: Say when the clock starts, how to find the right rows from the severity, and that privacy rows apply at any severity. Make the difference between Kestrel policy and law visible on every row, and require a log of each notice.

sections.heading: Internal escalation
sections.guidance: For each severity give who is told, by whom, within what time and by which channel, with names and IDs. Label every time as Kestrel policy. Include a row for any suspected privacy breach, because those start outside the security team.

sections.heading: Which law applies
sections.guidance: Explain that patient health information held by Kestrel as a custodian falls under the Health Information Act, while staff and other non-health personal information falls under the Protection of Privacy Act, and that one incident can trigger both.

sections.heading: Health Information Act duties
sections.guidance: State the duties exactly: affiliates tell the custodian; where there is a risk of harm, notify the Commissioner as soon as practicable, the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals, in writing to individuals. Include the narrow exception for withholding notice and that failing to notify is an offence. Cite only section 60.1 for this duty.

sections.heading: Protection of Privacy Act duties
sections.guidance: State the real risk of significant harm test (judged by a reasonable person), who must be notified and that it is without unreasonable delay. Say that below the threshold notice to the Commissioner and Minister is not required, and keep the two tests separate.

sections.heading: Suppliers and third parties
sections.guidance: For each vendor that holds or reaches Kestrel data, record the notice it owes Kestrel, labelling contract times as Kestrel contract requirements. Note the extra safeguards for information used outside Alberta.

sections.heading: Worked routing examples
sections.guidance: Run real incidents and the tabletop scenario through the matrix and show which Act and assessment each one triggers. If you cannot route a real case in one line, the matrix is not finished.

sections.heading: Records and review
sections.guidance: Say what the breach log records, who keeps it and how often the matrix and its phone numbers are tested and reviewed. An untested phone number fails at 03:00.

## How to use the matrix

- The clock starts when anyone at Kestrel, or a supplier, first becomes aware of the incident. Record that time.
- Find the severity in the incident classification model, then use the rows below. The privacy rows apply whatever the severity.
- Times marked Kestrel policy are internal rules proposed here. Duties marked with an Act are law.
- Log every notice: who, when, how and by whom.

## Internal escalation

| Severity | Who is told | By whom | Within (Kestrel policy, proposed) | Channel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | E-004, E-002, E-005, E-016, E-003 | Sam Okafor (E-020) | 15 minutes | Phone, then bridge call |
| Critical | Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), who briefs the executive and board | E-004 | 1 hour | Phone |
| High | E-004, the system custodian; E-003 if data is involved | E-020 | 1 hour | Phone and ticket |
| Medium | Resolver group; E-004 in the daily summary | E-020 | 4 hours | Ticket |
| Low | Security queue; weekly report | E-020 | Next business day | Ticket |
| Any suspected privacy breach | Privacy Office (E-003) | Whoever finds it, through their manager or the desk | Same shift | Phone or privacy form |

## Which law applies

- Patient health information Kestrel holds as a custodian: the Health Information Act (HIA).
- Staff and other non-health personal information, such as Identity Directory accounts or HR records: the Protection of Privacy Act (POPA). POPA does not apply to health information held by a custodian.
- One incident can involve both. Assess each kind of information under its own Act.

## Health Information Act duties

- An affiliate must tell the custodian (section 60.1). Affiliates include employees, contractors, students, volunteers and information managers, and Kestrel stays responsible for them.
- Kestrel must notify the Information and Privacy Commissioner as soon as practicable where there is a risk of harm to an individual as a result of the loss of, or unauthorized access to or disclosure of, health information.
- Kestrel must also notify the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals. Notice to individuals is in writing.
- The test is risk of harm, a lower bar than POPA's real risk of significant harm. The factors are set in the Health Information Regulation.
- Notice to an individual may be withheld only if it could reasonably be expected to harm that person's mental or physical health; Kestrel must then tell the Commissioner.
- Failing to notify is an offence under the Act.
- Kestrel policy (proposed): Priya Raman (E-003) completes the risk-of-harm assessment within 24 hours of the report, with facts from E-004, and the Privacy Office sends every notice.

## Protection of Privacy Act duties

- Where a reasonable person would consider that there is a real risk of significant harm to an individual from the loss of, or unauthorized access to or disclosure of, personal information, Kestrel must notify the affected individual, the Commissioner and the Minister responsible under the Act, without unreasonable delay.
- Notices must meet the requirements set by regulation, which also lists the harm factors.
- Below that threshold, notice to the Commissioner and Minister is not required. Kestrel still records the incident and its reasons (Kestrel policy).

## Suppliers and third parties

| Supplier | Duty to Kestrel |
|---|---|
| Sentinel SOC Services (V-04), logs processed in the United States | Report any incident involving Kestrel data within 24 hours (Kestrel contract requirement, proposed); HIA section 60 safeguards for information used outside Alberta |
| Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01), NorthArc Cloud (V-02) | Same notice clause; NorthArc holds the backups |
| ClearPath Staffing (V-03) | Report a lost device or misuse by its nurses the same day |
| Lumen Analytics Partners (V-05) | Notice clause survives contract end on 2026-11-30 |

Police: the executive decides on reporting extortion or other crime (Kestrel policy).

## Worked routing examples

| Case | Information involved | Route |
|---|---|---|
| SEC-003 unauthorized access to the Clinical Information System (A-001) | Patient health information | HIA risk-of-harm assessment by E-003 |
| SEC-009 unauthorized access to the Identity Directory (A-007) | Staff account data | POPA assessment; HIA too if health information was reached |
| SEC-005 lost device, email (A-013) | Depends on the mailbox and whether the device was encrypted | Assess under both Acts |
| Tabletop: the Clinical Information System encrypted at 07:00 | Patient records | Possible HIA breach until analysis shows whether health information was accessed, copied or lost |

## Records and review

- The Privacy Office keeps a breach log: discovery time, assessment, decision and reasons, notices sent and dates.
- The matrix is reviewed after the tabletop exercise and once a year, and phone numbers are tested every quarter (Kestrel policy, proposed).
mistakes: Using the POPA test for patient information. The Health Information Act test is risk of harm, a lower bar than real risk of significant harm, so applying the wrong test can skip a required notice.
Notifying only the Commissioner. Under the Health Information Act, Kestrel must also notify the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals.
Presenting Kestrel's internal times, such as 15 minutes or 24 hours, as law. They are Kestrel policy or contract terms and must be labelled that way.
Waiting for a full investigation before telling the Privacy Office. The assessment needs the facts early; the Health Information Act asks for notice as soon as practicable.

items.purpose: The vulnerability-remediation plan ranks Kestrel's open vulnerabilities by risk to patient care, sets fix dates against Kestrel's remediation policy, handles the hard cases (an invalid score, an unknown asset, an unsupported system) through owned exceptions, and defines how fixes are verified and reported. Sam Okafor (E-020), owner of WP-114, writes it from khn_security_events.csv and the system inventory; system custodians and business owners carry out and accept the actions; Daniel Osei (E-004) approves it and any risk acceptance. It is reviewed weekly. It practises the CISSP Security Operations domain (patch and vulnerability management) and Asset Security (end of support).

sections.heading: Scope, sources and data checks
sections.guidance: Give the counts (records, valid, open, overdue) at the as-of date and every data problem with its handling: the invalid CVSS score kept on the list, the unknown asset, the casing fix, and remediated items with no evidence dates. Never drop a dangerous finding because its record is messy.

sections.heading: Prioritization method
sections.guidance: Explain the policy windows, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity bands and the extra factors that turn a score into risk to patient care: tier, data class, remote code execution, patch availability, exposure. State the ordering rule so anyone can reproduce the ranking.

sections.heading: Open vulnerabilities
sections.guidance: One table of open findings with rank, system and tier, severity and score, due date with its window, and days overdue or remaining at the as-of date. Then explain any rank that is not obvious from the score, such as a lower score ranked higher because of the data it exposes.

sections.heading: Remediation actions
sections.guidance: For each finding give a concrete action, a named owner and a proposed date, and say which go through emergency change. Use the custodian from the inventory as the default owner of the technical fix, and say why when you choose someone else, for example to keep Kevin Park (E-009) from removing rights in the directory he administers.

sections.heading: Exceptions and compensating controls
sections.guidance: Where a fix is not possible yet, record why, the compensating controls, who accepts the remaining risk (the business owner, advised by the Chief Information Security Officer) and when it is reviewed. An exception without an end date is just a missed deadline.

sections.heading: Verification and closure
sections.guidance: Define what evidence closes a finding (rescan or configuration check, attached evidence, owner confirmation) and apply it to items already marked remediated.

sections.heading: Reporting and governance
sections.guidance: Say what is reported weekly and to whom, how overdue items escalate, how the plan relates to the Release 3 task and work package, and which process fixes stop the same data problems recurring.

## Scope, sources and data checks

Source: khn_security_events.csv, 10 vulnerability records, 9 valid; 8 open; 3 past due on 2026-10-01 (SEC-012, SEC-015, SEC-017).
- SEC-017 has a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score of 11.5, outside the 0.0 to 10.0 range, so it is not a valid record until rescored. It stays on this plan: a Critical remote code execution finding does not disappear because its score is wrong.
- SEC-016 is on A-021, which is not in the system inventory.
- SEC-019's severity "hIGH" is mapped to High.
- SEC-011 (Critical, A-008) and SEC-019 (High, A-005) are remediated, but the file holds no remediation dates, so closure evidence is requested.

## Prioritization method

1. Kestrel policy window from detection: Critical 7 days, High 30, Medium 60, Low 90.
2. CVSS base score: Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9, Critical 9.0 to 10.0. It rates technical severity, not risk.
3. Risk to patient care: system tier, data class, remote code execution (a common ransomware entry), whether a patch exists, exposure.
4. Overdue items first, then the rest by those factors.
The Health Information Act (HIA) section 60 requires safeguards against reasonably anticipated threats; leaving known Critical and High findings past their dates weakens that position.

## Open vulnerabilities

PACS is the Picture Archiving and Communication System; CIS is the Clinical Information System.

| Rank | Finding | System (tier) | Severity, CVSS | Due (window) | On 2026-10-01 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SEC-017 Remote code execution | A-004 PACS (2) | Critical, 11.5 invalid | 2026-09-28 (7 d) | 3 days overdue |
| 2 | SEC-012 Missing patch | A-001 CIS (1) | High, 8.1 | 2026-09-25 (30 d) | 6 days overdue |
| 3 | SEC-015 End-of-support software | A-014 Paging (1) | High, 8.6 | 2026-08-19 (30 d) | 43 days overdue |
| 4 | SEC-014 Excessive permission | A-007 Identity Directory (1) | High, 7.5 | 2026-10-15 (30 d) | 14 days left |
| 5 | SEC-016 Missing patch | A-021 unknown | Medium, 6.5 | 2026-11-07 (60 d) | 37 days left |
| 6 | SEC-020 Excessive permission | A-010 warehouse (2) | Medium, 5.4 | 2026-11-28 (60 d) | 58 days left |
| 7 | SEC-013 Weak cipher | A-013 Email (2) | Medium, 5.9 | 2026-11-01 (60 d) | 31 days left |
| 8 | SEC-018 Weak cipher | A-011 Service management (2) | Low, 3.7 | 2026-12-21 (90 d) | 81 days left |

Ranks 1 to 3 run in parallel now; rank decides who gets shared administrator time and change windows first. The CIS ranks above paging because its restore has failed twice, so an attack there is the hardest to recover from. SEC-020 ranks above SEC-013 because warehouse staging holds Restricted data.

## Remediation actions

| Rank | Action | Owner | Date (proposed) |

| 1 | Rescore; treat as Critical meanwhile. Limit PACS access to imaging devices and reading stations; vendor patch by emergency change | Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | 2026-10-05 |
| 2 | Test the Meridian (V-01) patch outside production; verified backup first; emergency change with downtime procedure | Kevin Park (E-009) | 2026-10-08 |
| 3 | No patch exists: isolate A-014, allow only paging flows, admin from the management zone only, extra monitoring | Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | 2026-10-07 |
| 4 | Remove excess directory rights; check against issue I-01 | Daniel Osei (E-004) | 2026-10-15 |
| 5 | Identify A-021, name an owner, register it, then patch; isolate it if no owner by the date | Sam Okafor (E-020) | 2026-10-09 |
| 6 | Remove excess warehouse rights | Tomás Rivera (E-006) | 2026-11-27 |
| 7, 8 | Disable weak ciphers through NorthArc Cloud (V-02) | Ahmed Haddad (E-017) | 2026-10-30, 2026-12-18 |

## Exceptions and compensating controls

- SEC-015: end of support passed 2026-06-30 and no patch will come. Time-bound risk acceptance by the business owner, Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), advised by Daniel Osei (E-004), with the rank 3 controls in place; review 2026-12-17 (proposed). Replacement goes to the residual risk register.
- SEC-016: no acceptance is possible until the system has an owner who can judge its impact.
- SEC-017: severity stays Critical until rescored.
An exception never extends a date silently: it has an owner, an end date and a recorded approver.

## Verification and closure

A finding closes only when a rescan or configuration check shows it fixed, the evidence is attached in the IT Service Management Platform (A-011), and the system owner confirms the service works. Attach rescan evidence for SEC-011 and SEC-019 now.

## Reporting and governance

- Weekly to Daniel Osei: open findings by severity, overdue count, age and exceptions. Baseline: 8 open, 3 overdue.
- Escalation (Kestrel policy, proposed): at the due date to the CISO; at twice the window to Marcus Bell (E-002).
- Release 3 task 24 (2026-11-27 to 2026-12-07, WP-114, CAD 80,000) covers the remaining findings and the process fixes: a CVSS range check at intake and every scanned asset mapped to the inventory. Overdue findings do not wait for it.
mistakes: Removing SEC-017 from the list because its CVSS score of 11.5 is invalid. The record needs rescoring, but a Critical remote code execution finding on a clinical system still needs action.
Ranking purely by CVSS score and ignoring the system: a High on the Clinical Information System or an unsupported tier 1 paging system matters more to patient care than the number alone shows.
Waiting for the Release 3 vulnerability task to start on 2026-11-27 while three findings are already past their due dates.
Marking SEC-015 as "cannot fix" with no compensating controls, accepted risk owner or review date.
